games.eco: D52 · Trung pháo hữu trực xa đối hậu bổ liệt pháo
notes: 20120315 2010 cnsc Round 9 Wang Ruixiang L Zheng Yihong Wang Ruixiang is a relative new comer. This is one of the longest game that I have translated and annotated. The game goes back and forth and then back and forth and then back and forth again...whew. Praise must be given to the two players for playing such an exciting game.

Wang Ruixiang is a relative new comer. GM Zheng Yihong opted to use this opening to prevent playing the more familiar openings that Wang might have studied and had flying daggers prepared. GM Zheng Yihong chooses to delay the battleground till midgame with this opening. The Opposite Direction Cannons was once popular in the 1980's but has gradually fallen out of favor.
This is one of the ways that red can play. A more aggressive approach would be to play R2+6 and it would be filled with fireworks.
C8+4 is another option, so that the opening can be directed back toward the more popular left cannon blockade opening for black.
And if black accepts the the offer, red would have increased his lead and have a one move advantage.

Although it seems that black can be satisfied with this outcome, red's R8+6 is very aggressive. Wang does not care about black playing R4=7 and shows his determination with this move. E3+1 would be the move to make if red opted for a more stable formation.

Post-game commentary suggested that this was not very ideal. When playing the ODC, you tell your opponent that you are going to fight tooth for tooth. By playing C5-1 just does not seem to conform to the spirit of the ODC. (post game commentary by Master Huang Hailin and GM Zhao Xinxin, not me...LOL). The commentary went on to state that whichever side is not brave or fearless enough would suffer losses...

Post game analysis suggests that this is the first move that leads to red's downfall. At this stage, red's third file is much superior than black's formation, hindering the development of black's left flank. By playing this move, red actually surrenders this advantage to black.

It is obvious that after losing the pawn on the 3rd file, he is suddenly under attack and has surrendered his lead to black. With this exchange of chariots, it can seen that red hopes for a draw now as the game enters a chariotless midgame.
At this stage, both sides have equivalent material but the position of all the black pieces are much better than red.
And entering midgame, the positions of the black pieces have just become better. The horses that black have would be worth more than the cannons that red have should the game enter endgame.
Red tries to hold on to his last lifeline. If the central pawn is lost, everything is lost. Red also tries to set a trap for black...
and black does NOT take the central pawn! This is because GM Zheng has seen through red's intentions.
Another controversial move from red. Red throws himself into the pits again with this move.
Red thinks that black's P5+1 is to block the red horse to allow himself to play P7+1, so he reacts with E1+3. But GM Zheng has a surprise in store...
And all of tha sudden, red's defenses fall apart...
Ouch...Red is forced to play this move. Click on the variation to see the catastrophe that would follow should he play K5-1
And red is still unable to prevent the powerful central pawn from advancing forward. Red's days are numbered... or is it so...?
At this stage, black has the huge advantage and is poised to win the game... BUT, perhaps the GM let his guard down and played this move, giving red a chance to redempt himself!

After a series of moves, red has pinned 3 of black's pieces on the pawn rank with one cannon. The poor position of the black king is another cause of worry. At this stage, one would think that perhaps a draw was possible!

Black retreats the horse to protect the all important central pawn. However, although black has 3 more effective pawns than red, all his pieces are now pinned, and it would stil be some time before black is able to win.

And red makes another fatal mistake, tilting the game in the other direction again. Post-game commentary states that red is trying to for a draw now and with this move he attempts to delete the material advantage that black has. However, in his haste, he plays this move. C4+3 would have been a much more aggressive move. As it would still be some time before the black pawns cross the river, there would be no need to try to take them out now.
Ouch, time trouble causes GM Zheng to play this move instead of P7+1!
And black is forced to give up the advantage he has built up thus far.
And red continues to try to force a draw by offering this exchange.
And at this point in time, the chances for a draw are very high. The game is now a test of endgame prowess for both sides.

And Red makes a mistake with this move. Post game commentary suggests that Red has not fully comprehended the key points of this endgame. The top priority should be to prevent the black 7th pawn from crossing the river. Red was rash to play this move. Perhaps he thinks that he could go for a win.
And black recollects himself after losing the huge advantage he had. A very good play from black, disallowing E9+7!
And after crossing the river, suddenly, black's chances of a win increase exponentially. Red's future looks dim. If red were to force a draw, it would take a lot of hard work!
Red tries to prevent the black cannon from maneuvering to the other side...
Ouch again... That ouch is not only for red's missed attempt at a win, but also for my aching fingers and eyes... PS: The above moves were less than half the actual number of moves played...
After GM Zheng had calmed down and recollected, his shows great Xiangqi kungfu with the adjustment of his defenses over the past few moves. Slowly, he tilts the game in his favor with these moves.
And after the past few rounds, black has slowly increased his lead again. Unknowingly, black has pinned red again and is slowly maneurvering his pawns forward for the final kill.
GM Zheng shows great patience and after a flurry of punches, he knocks out the red pawn, thereby ensuring a definite win now!
Finally, after approaching 100 moves, black makes a definite charge!

A better move would be P6+1 using that pawn to exchange for 2 advisors. The position of the red horse is undesirable, and black would have gained speed in attacking. This central cannon move is a more steadfast move. Perhaps time trouble has lead black to play more cautiously.

Theoretically, by moving the black cannon here, black could play H9-8 to attack the other horse and then concentrate his forces on red's right flank. However, post game commentary suggests that black has actually made a big mistake, albeit unnoticeable.
And both sides take a breather. The clock is still clicking on!

According to the rules, there was a 60 move limit on repetitive moves. Black was able to control the red pieces but red hung on and fought voraciously. Time is running out for black and he needs to capture material or the game would be ruled a draw.

For fear of the 60 move limit coming to an end, and that red has smartly maneuvered his horse out of a corner, black is forced to exchange his pieces so that a new 60 move limit could occur. However, his remaining black pawn is now a low pawn and it would greatly increase the difficulty required for a win.
And suddenly, after the red horse has been able to return to the center to help defend, a drawish game situation arises , again...
This time, time pressure causes red to make a mistake. H3-5 would have defended nicely!
Ouch again... The final move, I swear, that causes red the game. Heartbreaking for red!

And black steals the game with this move... Red resigns. If red H5-3, black would checkmate with P5+1. The red cannon cannot move and the last movable piece for red would be A6-5, whereby the red horse would be lost. The endgame would then be simplified now to a SURE WIN situation. Black wins this one after a hard fought battle. This game has gone back and forth but red has shown superb resiliency with a never give up attitude while black shows the patience steadfastness of a GM.

games.eco: C36 · Trung pháo quá hà xa hỗ tiến thất binh đối bình phong mã tả mã bàn hà
notes: sg 20120220 Wudangshan Cup Zhao Xinxin W Zheng Yihong C36 Central Cannon with Pawn Ranked Chariot with 7th Pawn Advancement vs Screen Horse Defense with 7th Pawn Advancement and Left Riverbank Horse variation. ECCO:C36 ????????????????? The 2010 Wudangshan Cup was a national event held in April 2010. There was a group tournament and an individual's section. 18 teams from 14 provinces took part in the team event and after 9rounds of competition in 4 days, the star studded team consisting Hong Zhi, Jiang Chuan, Wang Yang and Zhang Qiang were champions. In the individual's section, GM Liu Dahua came in first with an undefeated record of 5W4D0L. 2nd --> Jiang Chuan, 3rd,--> Zhang Qiang, 4th--> Zhao Xinxin , 5th --> Meng Chen, 6th --> Huang Zhufeng In this game, GM Zhao does badly in the opening and only manages to overturn the tables in the midgame after GM Zheng falls into time trouble.
Zhao Xinxin, one of the top ranked Xq players (consistently in top 10) in China today.
GM Zheng goes for this very violent variation! Always full of fireworks.

GM Zhao chooses to play it safe with this move. One of the most fireworked filled variations is to play P5+1. Perhaps GM Zhao fears that GM Zheng has something in the back of his pocket...and chooses this variation instead!
H7+5 is another viable option, allowing black to retain his 7th file pawn.
GM Zhao chooses to keep things complicated with this move so that he still has his chances.
This is a more proactive move from black. It allows the cannon to move to the left flank for a concentrated attack on red's right side or from the center with C2=5.
Another possibility is to play R9=8. In retrospect, R9=8 would seem better for red!
Good move! Black pins red's cannon rank with this move. Black prepares to play C8=5 and then capture the horse with the chariot.
Red is forced to sacrifice the elephant to try to keep his lead.
Post game analysis suggests E3-1 as a better move as not much is done with this attempted capture of the cannon.
Black insists on controlling this rank with this brilliant move!
Very versatile and lively play from black! Black suddenly shifts his focus to red's left flank, preparing to play C2=1 on the next move. Red is under much pressure!
Post game analysis showed that this was not as good as C6=8!!!

At this stage, although black is better off, time trouble starts to appear. Post-game commentary noted that GM Zheng started to rush his moves. Although better off, GM Zhao's chariot was just superb in defense, disallowing black any immediate chance of attack.
And after the exchange, the pressure on red's right side is relieved...time to turn the tables!
GM Zheng is in time trouble now and makes this move, costing him the game... R2-4 to pin the red horse and chariot would be much better, slowing the pace of red's attack!
And red captures the black horse with this move! Red has a deadly kill with H5+7!!!
And black loses. The moves end here! Red has forked black's cannon and chariot and has the superior pawn advantage, while black is in time trouble.

games.eco: A16 · Phi tượng tiến thất binh đối tiến hữu mã
notes: sg Zhao Guorong W Cai Yi A16 Elephant with 7th Pawn Advancement vs Right Proper Horse This game was played on 2011/11/23 between GM Zhao Guorong and Master Cai Yi. GM Zhao needs no introduction. Master Cai Yi ?? (born in 1984) is of Manchurian descent and majored in Law in Beijing's university. Master Cai is one of the hottest players in the past 5 years with a very good winning percentage. It was the ninth round in the competition and both players had already ammassed 11 points. Although it would be impossible to win the tournament, a win here would enable a good placing while a loss would mean a very poor placing, thus affecting the rankings that year. Commentary was provided by GM Wang Bin and this annotated game was found in the 12th Edition of the monthly Periodical Qiyi.

This is not a move that is often played. GM Zhao chooses to travel the less beaten path, and thus avoid any traps or flying daggers that Master Cai Yi would have prepared. With this move, GM Zhao wants the game to proceed to the midgame stage early.
So far the moves are ok. GM Wang Bin feels that this cross river chariot move does not seem to too proactive. He suggests that red push the central pawn forward instead.
And it is a standoff at this stage with red maintaining the slight advantage.
C2-2 would seem to a be a better move. By playing C2-2, red's lame horse (H2+4) is still a target for attack.
and both sides exchange their major pieces in the last few moves... The game has quickly progressed into midgame...

And the game quickly simplifies into the endgame stage. In the endgame, black has a horse which is more valuable than the cannon but it is undeveloped! Red also has more pawns and is already applying pressure to black's empty right flank. Advantage goes to red! Black would have a hard time even trying for a draw!
GM Zhao shows his prowess with this move!
Not a very efficient move. Post-game commentary suggests that black should play R8=5 to try to eliminate to try to offset red's pawn advantage.
GM Zhao does not rush his moves and answers patiently with this move.

Nice move! Black is in a dilemma now! Red forces the black chariot away from the riverbank. If black accepts the challenge, the board would simplify into a sure-win situation for red! The 3 red pawns alone would be sufficient to win black's full guard.
GM Wang Bin suggest R2-1 as another possible option as black can follow up this move with R2=4.
For unknown reasons, black opted to change his moves! If he continued to harrass the central elephant with R2-1 and repeating with R2+1, it was ok by the rules and could very well have forced a draw!
GM Zhao chooses to play it safe by changing his defensive formation. However, P5+1 is a good option as red already has superior material advantage!
Black is forced to make this move!
Red does not forget to prevent black's pawn from crossing the river!
And the final red pawn has crossed the river!!! If H5-3, red would capture the horse with a discovered check with P5=4 followed by P4=3.
And black resigns. Red wins.

games.eco: C93 · Ngũ bát pháo hỗ tiến tam binh đối bình phong mã
notes: sg 20120229 2010 jjls Liu Dahua W Hao Jichao C93 58 Cannons with 3rd Pawn Advancement vs Screen Horse Defense with 3rd Pawn Advancement ECCO:C93 ??????????? "Old" GM Liu Dahua, born in 1950, has been a force to reckon with for the past 40+ years. He was the man who stopped GM Hu Ronghua's 10 time winning streak. GM Liu was also consecutive National Champion in 1980,1981. Also known as the Oriental Computer, he set the record for 1 vs 19 in a blindfold Xq match in 1995. This record was only recently broken by GM Jiang Chuan (see bio and facts). GM Liu is still very active in the Xiangqi world in China and has maintained decent rankings consitently. He still wins a lot of tournaments. Master Hao Jichao, is another Xq star on the rise. Born in 1985 and a native of Harbin City, he has slowly worked his way up the ladder, making Master by coming in at 17th place in the 2009 Chinese National Singles Competition. I have chosen this game because it was one of the most exciting games that I have seen in the past month. Master Hao mounts a very fierce attack and even nearly wins, before making a fatal mistage. And GM Liu seized the opportunity to win. Very very exciting. For those new to ECCO, ECCO does not take into consideration the which side the first move is made, so although GM Liu plays C8=5, it is still recognized by ECCO as C2=5.
Master Hao plays the pawn first so that red cannot play Central Cannon with 7th Pawn Advancement.
By playing the ranked chariot, black opts for a very aggressive counter. Other commonly played variation include P9+1 and E3+5
There is also a R1+1 variation for red. Click on the variation below.
Correct move for black. It is not advisable to play C7+6 now!
R2=4 is another suggested move!
At this stage, both sides are entangled but red still holds the slight lead.
And a heart stopping battle begins! Master Hao draws first blood with this chariot exchange!
GM Liu wants to win it bad, and makes the first mistake. By capturing the elephant, he actually helps Master Hao from moving his king out to a position where he is safe.
And GM Liu uses up two moves with this chariot to try to capture the black horse. Red's left flank is empty...and black draws blood again...
Post game analysis suggests that red can play R3+5 and it would seem that he would have more chances !
To get rid of the threat the horse poses, red has used 3 chariot and one cannon moves, while at this time, black has been mounting his attack.
Red is faced with a do or die situation. A slight mistake and black would win!
Correct move. Post game analysis indicates that if the central pawn were not captured,black would be unable to win the game. Unfortunately, my manual does not show why... LOL
Instead of playing this move, and allowing red a breather, it was suggested that black play C1=4 instead! Black would still have the better prospects.
BLUNDER!!! Post game analysis suggests that this is the beginning of the end for black. Black fears the red horse from crossing the river...
FATAL BLUNDER! Post game analysis suggests that this is the move that cost black the game.
Black resigns! The comment was Master Hao played a good first half, but made a fatal mistake at the end... For beginners...click on to understand why black resigned...
and red would torture black to death...

games.eco: D54 · Trung pháo tả trực xa đối hậu bổ liệt pháo
notes: sg 20120229 jjls Hong Zhi L Jin Song This was a game played on 2010/08/14 by Red's GM Hong Zhi against black's Master Jin Song. GM Hong Zhi needs no introduction. He is still one of the top 10 players in China today, and has represented China in many competitions abroad. Master Jin Song was born in 1974, and hails from Shenyang,Liaoning Province. His greatest claim to fame was by winning a competiion held in 1998 by the AXF. He maintains a high winning percentage and amassed 2454 points in 2010. Master Jin remains a very powerful force and is one of the key players on the Shenyang Xiangqi team

Master Jin is an expert on the reserved opposite direction cannons counter. With this opening, he has won against many many experts. When going up against an opponent of GM Hong Zhi's caliber, it was natural for Master Jin to use this opening.
C8=7 is another commonly played variation.
Post-game analysis suggested that this move did not do much. R8=6 seemed to be a better choice as red would still have full control of the game.
Postgame analysis deemed this as another redundant move with not much purpose. H3+2 to maintain balanced development of the chess pieces seemed to be a better move.
Red chooses to develop his bottom chariot by R1=4.
And black forces an exchange. After the exchange, red's cannon would become an obvious target for black attack.

By playing the riverbank horse, red actually crowds his own chesspieces! The riverbank horse has not many places to go other than to protect the red cannon. H4+6 is not feasible as the black horse is protecting that intersection. It also impedes the red chariot. Post-game analysis suggests that red sacrifices the cannon to play R4+5, before winning forking and winning back material with R4=7.

And both polayers readjust their formations in the previous few moves. Post-game analysis of the game shows that after readjusting, red does NOT have any specific target to attack and the linking of the pieces are less than satisfactory. Black on the other hand, has a very stable defensive formation, and is one pawn up. At this stage, black has gained control of the game from red!

Post game analysis deemed this move as less than satisfactory. Even though red's formation is not good, preventing the black pawn from charging forward would be more important than development of the chess pieces now. By playing this move, red actually allows black's pawn to wreck havoc. Of all the moves, this play by red should shoulder most of the responsibility for red's loss.
Red just made his condition worse. P3+3 would still enable red to last sometime. Red played this move as a gamble to attack.
R8+3 is another viable alternative. Red would also be in trouble.
And red resigns.

And black is still able to hold his own!
And red would have good prospects and control of the game.

games.eco: E38 · Tiên nhân chỉ lộ chuyển tả trung pháo đối tốt để pháo phi tả tượng
notes: sg 20120304 2010 A league Zhu Xiaohu W Zhao Xinxin E38 Angel's pawn with Left Central Cannon variation vs Thundering Defense with Left Elephant Variation ECCO:E38 ??????????????? Master Zhu Xiaohu is another up and coming star in Xiangi. Born in 1985 his first claim to fame was in 2000, when he became the Chinese National Under 14 Champion. He was also a key player whne the Jiangsu team came in 6th place in 2008. GM Zhao Xinxin needs no further introduction. I have chosen this board because the opening is very interesting. Had GM Zhao drawn or won, his final placings might be very different!
So far so good...all textbook moves...

Out of the blue, Master Zhu plays this move! It is not in accordance to opening theory, but Master Zhu seems to be very well versed in this opening. For beginners, taking the central pawn is not advisable as black can easily chase it away. After taking the central pawn, red would often need another 1-2 moves to protect this cannon, thereby using up 3 moves early into the game, and delaying the development of the other pieces.
This is a more stable approach to the game. Click on the variation below to see other variations.
this is a commonly played variation
And this is a relatively new opening for both sides.

This was the actual move played by GM Zhao. C3+1 was played in another game. GM Zhao chose to be aggressive in hope of earning more points to improve his rankings. C3+1 would still to be to red's advantage, so GM Zhao took a risk with this move. Post-game analysis suggests that GM Zhao should not have played this variation.

Good play from red! By chasing away the black horse, red allows his own horses greater space for maneuvering. Once the horses are able to join in the battle, red would have better control of the game.

At this stage, although both red and black are similar in material (black has two pawns that has not crossed the river), all of the red chess pieces are very mobile and can attack from many directions. Black's pieces on the other hand are very congested, and it would take more time and effort just to develop them. The extra two black pawns remained undeveloped and are non-functional at this stage. But red still has some way to go before winning!
good move1 Red restricts the moved ment of the black horse and allows his left cannon to traverse to the right side for a concentrated attack.

!!Good move. This cannon move does many things. 1) attempt to gain a cannon and a horse in exchange for it 2) pinning the king should it come out to try to escape red's H3+4 followed by H4+3 for the elbow horse check. 3) prevents the black horse from moving H6+4 to attempt a counter of his own.the black horse cannot to anywhere important now after this move.
Black is forced to give up material. If he did not play this move, red would play H3+4 and black would be in deep trouble!
And within a short span of a few moves, red gains material and forces black to defend like crazy.

GM Zhao does not give up so easily though! Red must not be allowed to bring the horse across the river. The black pawns are still too far to have any effect on the game, so black focuses on defense first.
Red tries to further simplify the endgame to his advantage.
Black is forced to accept the exchange, and with that, red eliminates any immediate danger of a counter from black by capturing the black horse.

And the endgame has simplified to 1r1h1c2a2e vs 1r1c2p2a2e. For red, it would be obvious that he has the upperhand. His main goal is to try to bring all his major pieces across the river for an attack. Black on the other hand must try to prevent this, and amongst the three pieces, the horse is the natural target for black. If the red horse were allowed to cross the river, it would be over. The following moves center around this line of thought.
And black puts up a strong defence. Red has trouble finding a weak point to attack for the moment.
And red attacks from the center!
Black tries too buy some time with the previous moves.
Red's horse can only retreat or be caught by the black horse. Great defense!
Black tries to go for a draw now.
And black continues his brilliant defense.
Red tries another approach...attacking from the sidelines.

And GM Zhao's defense has been brilliant thus far. The young Master Zhu is faced with a tough challenge. This sort of endgame is very challenging for red. Black's defense has been brilliant thus far but time is running out.
Post game analysis suggests that black play R4=5 to control the red horse. It would be more proactive than this move. Time is not to black's advantage.
Post game analysis suggests that black move C5=4 to defend and red would still have a hard time breaking through. This is a costly mistake. Red finally sees a chance. Red starts his final campaign.

And now the red horse is able to join in the attack. The main function of black's cannon at the baseline is to help defend the bottom rank and throat rank. Now, that function is lost and red goes on a rampage. The price to pay for black's C5=7 on move 76 is now evident. Black can hold on not much longer.

And red is almost assured of victory now. Red has successfully pinned the black chariot to the 4th file and the black cannon is functionless. Red can take his time to bully the black cannon and other defensive pieces with his chariot.
The last straw. Red attempts to capture the most important defensive piece now, the central advisor.

Black resigns after this move. The cannon is lost and so will the rest of black's defence. Postgame analysis noted that GM Zhao was too keen on winning and because he tried to keep things complicated, the risks he took caused him to be attacked by red's combination of 1r1h1c. And although his defense in endgame was tight, time pressure caused him to make mistakes and gradually caused him the game. Kudos to the young master Zhu Xiaohu.

games.eco: A31 · Phi tượng tiến hữu mã đối tả quá cung pháo
notes: sg 20120307 2010 jjls Pan Zhenbo L Zheng Weitong This is a short game played in 2010/9/29. He was awarded the title of Xiangqi Master in 1994 by coming in 10th place in the National Chinese Xiangqi Championships, and improving his placings to 4th place in 2004, before improving to 2nd place in 2005. notes: sg 20120603 1991 sdcking Hu Ronghua W Li Laiqun ECCO D11 Same Direction Cannons: Filed chariot vs slow chariot ECCO:D11 ???????? In 1991, an unusual competition was held. It was called the Baoren Cup Xiangqi World Same Direction Cannons competition. Players from all over the world were invited to take part. There was a catch, both red and black were only allowed to play the same direction cannons for the first move. The competition was held in Kunming China. GM Hu Ronghua eventually won the tournament, making him the first ever and last (no future such tournaments were held) Same Direction Cannons King of the World. The biggest obstacle to his crowning of the championship was GM Li Laiqun. They met in round 4 in this short but very exciting game held on 17th of Sept 1991. It was obvious that whoever won this game would have a big chance of claiming one of the most interesting titles in the history of Xiangqi. I found this board on the internet. Unfortunately, it was not known who had commented on this game.

Red H8+9 was a relatively fashionable variation way back then, 20 years ago. In the 70-80's the proper horses were the rage. By playing P7+1, black chose the slow variation or deferred variation as some might prefer to call it. Normally, black would play H2+3 but GM Li decides to play the ranked chariot, in the hope of bringing the game to relatively unchartered waters. Just from the first 4 moves, we can see how important this game was to both GMs.
And this move from red to attack the pawn rank is also seldomly seen. GM Hu shows his creativity in this one.

Black tries to gain some initiative with this move. However, R1+1 would have been better as in the ancient manuals, this move of black was frowned upon. Playing R1+1 would give black a more balanced game as his central cannon be moved away if need be. Playing C5=7 is not healthy for black now. Click on the variation below to understand why.
Correct move for black. Black has to remove or decreased the threat of this red chariot. Black would lose quickly if he played H3-5 now.
Nice move!!! Black is prevented from defending the advisor so that red can go for the kill with K5=4 quickly!
In retrospect, this was the move that lost the game for black. C4+1 is the suggested move.

Red pounces on black's mistake and attacks ferociously by advancing the chariot and playing the king. Black is in deep trouble. An interesting thing to note about this game is that after so many moves, all 32 chess pieces are still on the board, which is quite rare indeed! Black has choked his own king with the centroid (WXF term which refers to the position where the black central horse is). This would become a deciding factor in the game. Black's king and advisors are immobilized and thus made a sitting duck. Red does not worry about the possible attacks that black might have using his cannon on his chariots and adamantly plays his king to join in the attack. The reason for this is that he has been aiming to attack from the center for a long time!

Another interesting point to note about this game is that red only made his first pawn move after 21 moves. This is another very very rare situation. Red plays his pawn now to chase away the black chariot.

And black resigns. All of black's chess pieces are pinned by Red. Red threatens with a checkmate with C-+3 which would force black to defend with R2+2. The black cannon and chariot are also pinned by the red chariot. Black cannot afford to exchange the cannon for the horse with R6=7 or else red would simply win with the iron bolt checkmate! Black simply does not have any other chess piece to move! Red on the other hand can charge his pawn forward, or even his two horses, at his own pace for the final win. Very interesting game!
